intro.text: sections: Introduction to Interaction Design • Usability Goals • Prototyping Techniques • Heuristics for Understanding, Action and Feedback
Read the short explanation first, then study the illustration and chapter example. The goal is to understand the concept quickly for independent revision.

blocks.text: 01. Why interface design matters
THINK  Can you think of experiences where you have been left frustrated by the user interface of a website or an app? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

Most user stories require a user interface (UI) that implements the feature. The UI is the interaction point between the user and the system — web pages with buttons, text fields, navigation etc. The form of the product is what the user sees first, and only then its functionality; if the interface is not appealing or intuitive, users will reject it or find it extremely cumbersome. The key idea is to give the user a good experience: easy to use, easy to learn, not confusing.
What frustrates users: cluttered layout, no hierarchy, no navigation, poor typography, random use of colours, slow load time, too many ads, inconsistent colour scheme.

blocks.caption: What frustrates users vs a clean, well-organised UI.
blocks.alt: What frustrates users vs a clean, well-organised UI.

blocks.text: 02. The user interface is the interaction point
The UI is the interaction point between the user and the system.

In software companies, roles such as interaction designers and UX/UI developers look at these aspects. Interaction design means designing interactive products to support people in their everyday working lives.

blocks.caption: Figure 2. The user interface is the interaction point

blocks.text: 03. Four activities of interaction design

rows: Developing alternative designs that meet those requirements

blocks.text: This is similar to the Agile process, because both keep the user at the centre of creating the product. Techniques for developing alternative designs include storyboarding and paper prototyping.

blocks.caption: Figure 3. Four activities of interaction design

blocks.text: 04. Design in everyday objects and software

Ordinary everyday objects have gone through several rounds of discussion and deliberation to arrive at their final design. The illustration shows design decisions about a desk lamp, a drinking glass and a table.

blocks.caption: Everyday objects involve decisions about shape, stability, materials and construction.
blocks.alt: Everyday objects involve decisions about shape, stability, materials and construction.

blocks.text: Usability goals and user experience goals are related, but they are not identical.

rows: Positive emotions such as satisfying, enjoyable, fun, helpful, entertaining, motivating, emotionally fulfilling
More subjective — how users experience the product from their own perspective, rather than how useful or productive it is from the system's perspective

blocks.caption: Usability goals (centre) and user experience goals (outer ring) — after Jennifer Preece.
blocks.alt: Usability goals (centre) and user experience goals (outer ring) — after Jennifer Preece.

blocks.text: 05. Five usability goals
Usability (ISO 9241-11): The extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

rows: How good a system is at doing what it is supposed to do — is it capable of allowing people to learn well, carry out their work efficiently, access the information they need, buy the goods they want?
The way a system supports users in carrying out their tasks — common tasks through a minimal number of steps; once learned, users can sustain a high level of productivity.
Protect users from dangerous conditions and undesirable situations; help users avoid unwanted actions accidentally and provide recovery from errors.
How easy a system is to learn to use.
How easy a system is to remember how to use, once learned — especially important for systems used infrequently; users shouldn’t have to relearn tasks after months away.

blocks.caption: Figure 5. Five usability goals

blocks.text: 06. Effectiveness: doing the intended task
How good a system is at doing what it is supposed to do — is it capable of allowing people to learn well, carry out their work efficiently, access the information they need, buy the goods they want?
EXAMPLE  Google — minimal design with the main functionality (search) at the centre; Amazon — all necessary information (cost, delivery date, offers) on a single page, no need to scroll.

blocks.caption: Effectiveness: search at the centre and necessary shopping information together.
blocks.alt: Effectiveness: search at the centre and necessary shopping information together.

blocks.text: 07. Efficiency: reducing unnecessary effort
The way a system supports users in carrying out their tasks — common tasks through a minimal number of steps; once learned, users can sustain a high level of productivity.
EXAMPLE  Buying on Amazon — Buy Now → select delivery address → select payment method → buy; Amazon saves the delivery address and card details so returning users can buy quickly.

blocks.caption: Common tasks in a minimal number of steps.
blocks.alt: Common tasks in a minimal number of steps.

blocks.text: 08. Safety in safety-critical systems

Two aspects of safety. First: protecting the user from dangerous conditions and undesirable situations — e.g. user interfaces of X-ray machines and chemical plants. Therac-25 was a radiation therapy machine, first of its kind, with a dual treatment mode, using software-based safety systems rather than hardware controls. One day the operator pressed X (X-ray mode) instead of E (electron mode); this led to excess radiation and the death of a patient.

blocks.caption: Therac-25: pressing X instead of E.
blocks.alt: Therac-25: pressing X instead of E.

blocks.text: 09. Safety: avoid accidental actions

THINK  Recall software applications that you have used. How have they reduced the risk of wrong keys being pressed or provided a means of recovery after errors? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

Second: helping users in any situation avoid carrying out unwanted actions accidentally — reduce the risk of wrong keys being pressed. Example: in document software the Save and Close buttons are far apart.

blocks.caption: Save and Close are placed far apart.
blocks.alt: Save and Close are placed far apart.

blocks.text: 10. Safety: recovering from mistakes

Provide a means of recovery if users make errors: accidentally deleted a file → recover from trash; computer shut down while editing in Word → recovery options next time; Undo (Ctrl+Z); WhatsApp — delete a message sent by mistake.

blocks.caption: Figure 10. Safety: recovering from mistakes

blocks.text: 11. Learnability for new users
How easy a system is to learn to use. People want to get started right away without much effort — e.g. Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Amazon are learned without reading a manual.

blocks.caption: Figure 11. Learnability for new users

blocks.text: 12. Learning more complex tasks
THINK  What are ways in which you can help users learn how to use a complex system? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

For complex systems: Wizards — a step-by-step process that breaks a complex task into simpler tasks. Tours — highlight important areas or features of a page with lots of information, for new learners. Templates — provide defaults or structure for a specific type of task (e.g. a resume template), so you don't start from scratch.

blocks.caption: Wizards, tours and templates.

blocks.text: 13. Memorability versus user experience

How easy a system is to remember how to use, once learned — especially important for systems used infrequently; users shouldn’t have to relearn tasks after months away. Example: Microsoft Word — meaningful icons, command names and menu options help users remember where to find a tool.

Beyond usability, we want users to experience positive emotions — satisfying, enjoyable, fun, helpful, entertaining, motivating, emotionally fulfilling. These goals are more subjective and concern how users experience the product from their perspective.
Important distinction: memorability is a usability goal, while enjoyable or satisfying use belongs to user-experience goals.

blocks.caption: Figure 13. Memorability versus user experience

blocks.text: 14. Why not code the first design immediately?
THINK  Are we ready to code once we know the needs and requirements? Why shouldn’t we code the UI right away? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

Initial design ideas might not be the best ones. Developing an interface takes time, money and effort (if users don't like it, you redesign from scratch). Prototypes let you quickly test on users, get feedback, iterate and pivot.

blocks.caption: Figure 14. Why not code the first design immediately?

blocks.text: 15. Prototype, feedback and iteration
Prototypes answer questions and support designers in choosing between alternatives. Purpose: test out the technical feasibility of an idea; clarify vague requirements; user testing and evaluation.

blocks.caption: Figure 15. Prototype, feedback and iteration

blocks.text: 16. Levels of prototype fidelity

Prototypes differ by purpose, time of development and fidelity — how real the interface is compared to the final product. Storyboards and paper prototypes come early and don't resemble the final product much; digital mock-ups (e.g. Photoshop, PowerPoint) and interactive prototypes (e.g. a web app with fake data) move closer to it.

blocks.caption: Fidelity vs time — and what each prototype facilitates conversations about.
blocks.alt: Fidelity vs time — and what each prototype facilitates conversations about.

blocks.text: 17. Storyboard: setting, sequence, satisfaction

A hand-drawn comic featuring Setting + Sequence + Satisfaction. Setting: people involved, environment, task being accomplished. Sequence: what steps are involved, what leads someone to use the app, what task is illustrated. Satisfaction: what motivates people to use the system, what it enables people to accomplish, what need it fills.

blocks.caption: Figure 17. Storyboard: setting, sequence, satisfaction

blocks.text: 18. Storyboard example: Speak-Up
A virtual reality tool to help give effective presentations: simulates a presentation setting, records audio during the presentation, and provides hints.

rows: He has a presentation on Monday and practises in front of a mirror, but on the day he is nervous.
A friend recommends Speak-Up; he chooses the type of audience and records his audio; the system gives feedback and comments; he sends the recording to his mentor; a second round of practice.
He presents confidently in front of a large audience.

blocks.caption: Speak-Up storyboard: setting, sequence, satisfaction.

blocks.text: 19. Benefits of storyboards

Emphasizes how the interface accomplishes a task (without specific details); avoids commitment to a particular user interface (the storyboard communicates the task without implementing the application or committing to a detailed UI); shared understanding among stakeholders.

blocks.caption: Benefits of storyboards.

blocks.text: 20. How paper prototyping works
A hand-drawn interface using multiple pieces of paper for the different screens.

blocks.caption: Figure 20. How paper prototyping works

blocks.text: 21. Accessible digital-library paper prototype

Online library for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) and speech-impaired students — books in Indian Sign Language (ISL) and speech therapy. The first screen is login; the user can be a student, teacher or parent; clicking an option shows the next screen; choosing ISL opens a drop-down to choose the language.
Benefits: Easier than writing code for the UI; starts conversations about user interactions; elements can be changed immediately based on feedback.

blocks.caption: Paper screens show login, user type, resources and language selection.
blocks.alt: Paper screens show login, user type, resources and language selection.

blocks.text: 22. Paper prototype vs digital mock-up vs interactive prototype

Digital mock-ups use tools like PowerPoint, Photoshop or Figma and are closer to the final product; buttons and links can be clickable, and they can be shown to clients for feedback before moving to the final product.
Prototypes facilitate conversations: storyboards → user tasks; paper prototypes → user interactions; digital mock-ups → visual design; interactive prototypes → picky usability details.

blocks.caption: Figure 22. Paper prototype vs digital mock-up vs interactive prototype

blocks.text: 23. Two kinds of interface evaluation
THINK  What are ways in which you can evaluate the user interface of your prototype? Pause and write down your responses before reading further.

Ways to evaluate a UI: assess with real users; critique from expert designers — but that can be subjective, so specific guidelines help. Heuristics are strategies derived from previous experiences with similar problems — rules of thumb/guidelines. The most widely used set is Jakob Nielsen's 10 design heuristics; Prof. Scott Klemmer grouped them into Understanding, Action and Feedback.

blocks.caption: Figure 23. Two kinds of interface evaluation

blocks.text: 24. Consistency

Consistent layout — colour, font etc. consistent across all screens; e.g. in your operating system the Yes/No and Minimize/Restore/Close buttons are placed consistently across windows. Consistent names — product and feature names the same throughout.

blocks.caption: Figure 24. Consistency

blocks.text: 25. Familiar language and metaphors

Use words familiar to end users, not technical jargon — online shopping uses physical-store terms like checkout and shopping cart; paying online uses a 'mobile wallet' with actions like adding or removing money.

blocks.caption: Figure 25. Familiar language and metaphors

blocks.text: 26. Clean and functional design

Minimal and easy to understand. A cluttered design (many colours, fonts, images, no common theme) makes it hard to find information; a good design has clear navigation describing key features and consistent colours and fonts.

blocks.caption: Figure 26. Clean and functional design

blocks.text: 27. Overview of heuristic groups

Understanding = consistency, familiar language and metaphors, clean and functional design. Action = freedom, flexibility, recognition over recall. Feedback = show status, prevent errors, support error recovery, provide help.

blocks.caption: Design heuristics grouped into Understanding, Action and Feedback.
blocks.alt: Design heuristics grouped into Understanding, Action and Feedback.

blocks.text: 28. Freedom to undo or recover
Deleted a file → recover from trash; documents → recovery options; Undo — Ctrl+Z.

blocks.caption: Undo an edit, restore a deleted file, or recover an unsaved document.
blocks.alt: Undo an edit, restore a deleted file, or recover an unsaved document.

blocks.text: 29. Freedom to explore

Platforms should let users explore key features — online shopping lets you look at products without signing in. In the lecture's earlier IRCTC example, users could not search for trains without logging in, restricting their freedom; the later example allows searching without logging in.

blocks.caption: Figure 29. Freedom to explore

blocks.text: 30. Flexibility: beginner and expert methods
Flexibility means supporting different ways to complete the same task. New users use menus for cut/copy/paste in Microsoft Word or Google Docs; experts use keyboard shortcuts.

blocks.caption: Figure 30. Flexibility: beginner and expert methods

blocks.text: 31. Personalization versus customization

Personalization occurs when the system adapts content automatically for a user. Customization occurs when the user explicitly chooses settings or categories. Example: personalization — social media; customization — news apps asking which topics.

blocks.caption: Figure 31. Personalization versus customization

blocks.text: 32. Recognition over recall

Users have limited memory and find it easier to recognize something seen earlier — e.g. 'What is the capital of Spain?' vs 'Is Madrid the capital of Spain?'. Pre-GUI: moving a file in Linux needed mv temp.txt new_folder/; now: right-click on the file. Buttons and navigation should help users reach their goal: In the Google redesign example discussed in the lecture, the earlier product icons (e.g. Gmail's envelope shape) were easy to recognize; after the redesign all apps had the same colour and form, and many people found them hard to tell apart on small screens.

blocks.caption: Recognition over recall: visible actions and distinguishable app icons.
blocks.alt: Recall a file-move command versus recognise a menu action; distinct icons versus icons with a shared colour palette.

blocks.text: 33. Show system status
Keep users informed through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time — loading status in browsers; how much time an action will take (e.g. a download).

blocks.caption: Show loading status and the estimated time remaining.
blocks.alt: Show loading status and the estimated time remaining.

blocks.text: 34. Give next steps and advance warnings
Provide next steps (form signup, email signup) and warnings in advance (e.g. Gmail storage running out → buy storage).

blocks.caption: Figure 34. Give next steps and advance warnings

blocks.text: 35. Prevent errors with helpful constraints
Why do users make errors? We often blame the user, but aspects of the UI can lead users to make errors.
EXAMPLE  In a flight booking form, the return date cannot be before the 19 July departure; earlier dates are greyed out.

blocks.caption: Figure 35. Prevent errors with helpful constraints

blocks.text: 36. Prevent errors with suggestions
Offer suggestions — e.g. typing 'usability' in the browser, search auto-suggest gives a list of options.

blocks.caption: Typing usability produces suggestions that help users choose a query.
blocks.alt: Typing usability produces suggestions that help users choose a query.

blocks.text: 37. Support recovery after an error

Make the problem clear — on a signup form, clicking Sign Up with empty fields highlights each field in red. Provide a solution — a tooltip says to enter a valid email or mobile number. Provide an alternative — searching the misspelled 'Jacob Neilson', the search engine suggests the correct query.

blocks.caption: Make the problem clear, provide a solution, provide an alternative.
blocks.alt: Make the problem clear, provide a solution, provide an alternative.

blocks.text: 38. Provide searchable and contextual help

Ensure help is easy to search — most tools have a Help menu with help topics, trainings, updates. Provide help in context — e.g. in the Moodle LMS 'add a new course' form, a help icon next to fields like course visibility explains them exactly where and when needed.

blocks.caption: Searchable help and help beside the course-visibility field.
blocks.alt: Searchable help and help beside the course-visibility field.

blocks.text: 39. Heuristic evaluation by experts

After the initial prototypes are ready, experts evaluate the interface: they do multiple passes through the prototype and produce a list of issues that violate the design heuristics. Collecting feedback from several experts helps fix multiple usability issues. The heuristics are also a self-check for designers.

blocks.caption: Experts do multiple passes and list heuristic violations
blocks.alt: Experts do multiple passes and list heuristic violations

blocks.text: Interaction design cycle: Identify needs and requirements → Develop alternative designs → Build interactive versions → Evaluate.
Usability (ISO 9241-11): The extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use.
Usability goals: Effectiveness, Efficiency, Safety, Learnability, Memorability.
User experience goals: positive, subjective — satisfying, enjoyable, fun, helpful, entertaining, motivating, emotionally fulfilling.
Learnability for complex tasks: Wizards, Tours, Templates.

Safety: Therac-25 — the operator pressed X (X-ray mode) instead of E (electron mode); excess radiation led to the death of a patient. Save and Close buttons are placed far apart to prevent unwanted actions.
Memorability: meaningful icons, command names and menu options in Microsoft Word help returning users remember where tools are.
Storyboard = Setting + Sequence + Satisfaction.

Storyboard benefits: Emphasizes how the interface accomplishes a task (without specific details); avoids commitment to a particular user interface (the storyboard communicates the task without implementing the application or committing to a detailed UI); shared understanding among stakeholders.

Paper prototype: a hand-drawn interface using multiple pieces of paper for different screens. Benefits: Easier than writing code for the UI; starts conversations about user interactions; elements can be changed immediately based on feedback.
Prototypes facilitate conversations: storyboards → user tasks; paper prototypes → user interactions; digital mock-ups → visual design; interactive prototypes → picky usability details.
Heuristics are adapted from Jakob Nielsen and grouped by Scott Klemmer into Understanding, Action and Feedback.

Understanding = consistency, familiar language and metaphors, clean and functional design. Action = freedom, flexibility, recognition over recall. Feedback = show status, prevent errors, support error recovery, provide help.
Error recovery: make the problem clear / provide a solution / provide an alternative.

Heuristic evaluation: experts do multiple passes through initial prototypes and list design-heuristic violations; feedback from several experts helps fix usability issues. Heuristics are also a self-check for designers.
